title: LeaseBoston: Apartment Search Inside Claude
pitch: I built LeaseBoston, an MCP server that brings apartment search into Claude and ChatGPT. Renters see ranked listings as cards in the chat and can ask a landlord anything. If the landlord already answered, the saved answer comes back word for word. If not, the renter can send the question with one click, and the landlord replies from an inbox. Every reply can be saved, so the next renter gets it instantly. It has 29 tests and a demo recorded live in Claude Desktop.

components.name: MCP server
components.one_liner: The single door Claude and ChatGPT use to reach LeaseBoston
components.explain: I am the one MCP server, named leaseboston, that Claude or ChatGPT talks to. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way for a chat app to call tools. I offer five tools: search_apartments, get_apartment, ask_landlord, send_question_to_landlord and check_landlord_reply. I run over stdin/stdout for Claude Desktop and Claude Code, or over HTTP at /mcp for ChatGPT. I also give the model a short instruction text that tells it how to behave.
components.why: Every chat app sees only what I declare, so my tool types and instruction text decide whether the model behaves safely. Without my host check and transport choices, ChatGPT could not reach a laptop through a tunnel. Without the instructions, the model might guess a landlord's policy.

children.name: Two transports
children.one_liner: stdio for Claude, plain-JSON HTTP for ChatGPT
children.explain: I can start in two ways. With the stdio command I talk over stdin and stdout, the text pipes of a process, which Claude Desktop and Claude Code use. With the serve command I listen on HTTP at /mcp, port 8000 unless you pick another, which ChatGPT reaches through a tunnel. I pass json_response=True, so each reply is one plain JSON body instead of an SSE stream, a long-lived stream of events. I do this because Cloudflare quick tunnels do not support SSE, and no tool of mine needs streaming.
children.why: Claude and ChatGPT connect in different ways, so one server needs both doors. If I used a streaming reply, ChatGPT calls through the free Cloudflare tunnel would fail. Plain JSON works through the tunnel and costs nothing, because every tool answers in one shot.

children.name: Host guard
children.one_liner: Only localhost and the tunnel hostname may reach the server
children.explain: The MCP SDK ships a guard against DNS rebinding, a trick where a web page points its own host name at your laptop. By default the guard answers only localhost, written as 127.0.0.1, localhost and [::1]. When I start with --public-host, I add that tunnel hostname, with and without a port, to allowed_hosts. I also add its https origin to allowed_origins, and --allow-origin can add more. Any other Host header is refused.
children.why: A local server with no host check can be driven by a hostile web page open in the same browser. Opening it to one named tunnel host lets ChatGPT in without opening it to everyone. Without the flag, the tunnel's own host name would be refused.

children.name: Tool contracts
children.one_liner: Typed inputs and outputs the model can read and obey
children.explain: I write each tool's inputs with Python types: Annotated, Field and Literal. The SDK turns them into JSON Schema, a machine-readable list of allowed values, such as min_beds from 0 to 6. Each tool returns dict[str, Any], which gives structured output. components.name: In-chat card (MCP App)
components.one_liner: Search results and answers drawn as a card inside the chat
components.explain: I show results inside the chat as a card, a small web page the host draws in a locked-down box called a sandboxed iframe. The page is one file, app.html, with no outside scripts or fonts, because the default security policy would block them. It talks to the host with JSON-RPC (small JSON request and reply messages) sent over postMessage, following the 2026-01-26 spec. The tool result picks the view: matches become a carousel, and a status becomes an answer or a consent form. Both search_apartments and ask_landlord point at this card, and other hosts just get the same data as text.
components.why: Without a card, the renter would read long lists of listings as chat text. Keeping the card in one file with no network needs means it loads fast inside a sandbox. Hosts that ignore cards still work, because the same data comes back as text.

children.name: Handshake with the host
children.one_liner: JSON-RPC messages over postMessage tell the host who I am
children.explain: I talk to the host in JSON-RPC, small JSON envelopes with an id, a method and params, sent by window.parent.postMessage. Each request gets a number, and I park its resolve and reject callbacks in a pending map until the reply with that id arrives. On load I send ui/initialize with my app name, protocol version 2026-01-26 and empty capabilities, then ui/notifications/initialized once the host replies. The host pushes tool-input and tool-result notifications, and a ResizeObserver reports my size with size-changed whenever the page grows or shrinks. Any other host request, like a teardown or ping, gets an empty result back so the host never waits on me.
children.why: Without the pending map, a reply could not be matched to the question that caused it. Without the initialize step, the host would not know the card is ready for results. Without size-changed, the iframe would stay the wrong height.

components.name: Question lifecycle
components.one_liner: A reference code and four statuses carry each question to its answer
components.explain: I give every landlord question a short reference code and a status, and the status shows where it stands. A question starts as auto_answered when a saved answer matched, or not_sent when none did. It becomes waiting once the renter says yes and I send it, then replied when the landlord answers. The landlord's reply can also be saved as a new answer, so the next renter asking the same thing gets it instantly.
components.why: Each MCP call, one request from the model, arrives on its own, so the code and status are the only memory of a question. Without four clear statuses, I could not stop a double send or know when a reply is due.

children.name: Reference code
children.one_liner: Each question gets a short readable code the model passes back

The five characters come from 31 symbols with no 0, O, 1, I or L, so a code reads aloud cleanly. Each MCP call arrives alone, so I return the code and the model passes it back as a plain argument. children.name: Idempotent send
children.one_liner: Sending twice changes nothing: the second call returns the status

Email must look like name@host.tld, sms needs at least 10 digits, and app needs a non-empty username or email. If the question is already waiting or replied, I return that status and send nothing, so a repeated call never sends twice. Otherwise I set the status to waiting, email the landlord, and send the renter a confirmation on their channel. For chat_only nothing goes to the renter, because that channel means they will check back in the chat.

components.name: Answer matcher
components.one_liner: Finds the landlord's saved answer, or admits there is none.
components.explain: I decide whether a landlord already answered a renter's question, using plain code with no AI model. That means the same question always gets the same result. I turn each question into key words, then weigh each word by how rare it is across all saved questions. children.name: Accessibility driver
children.one_liner: Finds buttons by role and name, then acts on their refs
children.explain: I wrap the agent-desktop command-line tool in ad.run, which runs one command and parses its JSON reply. To find a control, I search the accessibility tree (the labelled list of buttons and fields an app exposes) by role and name. Each match carries a ref_id, a short handle that later click and type commands use as their target. A find that matches nothing still returns ok:true, so I count the matches instead of trusting the ok flag. To see if Claude is busy, I look for a 'Stop response' button every 1.5 seconds; two empty checks mean it is done.
children.why: If I trusted the ok flag, every search would look like a hit and the script would think Claude was always busy. It would then never move to the next scene. Searching by role and name also survives a button moving, where fixed screen coordinates would not.
